blurb.en: Say hello the local way, greet elders first, and close a talk politely.
blurb.sw: Kusalimia kama wenyeji, kuwaamkia wazee kwanza na kuaga kwa adabu.

blurb.en: Keep any conversation alive when you don't understand yet.
blurb.sw: Kuendeleza mazungumzo hata kama bado huelewi kila kitu.

blurb.en: Answer the first questions everyone asks: name, home, work, family.
blurb.sw: Kujibu maswali ya kwanza: jina, nyumbani, kazi na familia.

blurb.en: Ask prices, bargain fairly, count, pay and get change.
blurb.sw: Kuuliza bei, kupatana, kuhesabu, kulipa na kupata chenji.

blurb.en: Agree a fare, give directions to a driver and get off where you want.
blurb.sw: Kukubaliana kuhusu nauli, kumwelekeza dereva na kushuka unapotaka.

blurb.en: Get help fast, and handle the pharmacy and the doctor.
blurb.sw: Kupata msaada haraka, kemisti na daktari.

blurb.en: Order, say how you like it, and be a good guest at someone's table.
blurb.sw: Kuagiza, kusema unavyopenda na kuwa mgeni mwema mezani.

blurb.en: Visit a family home, honour the elders, and leave well.
blurb.sw: Kutembelea familia, kuwaheshimu wazee na kuaga vizuri.

blurb.en: Make a plan on the phone: when, where, and 'I'll call you back'.
blurb.sw: Kupanga kwenye simu: lini, wapi na nitakupigia.

blurb.en: Say how you are, talk about the day, and react like a friend.
blurb.sw: Kusema hali yako, kuongea kuhusu siku na kujibu kama rafiki.

blurb.en: Find the right matatu, agree the fare, and get off where you want.
blurb.sw: Kupata matatu sahihi, nauli na kushuka mahali unapotaka.

blurb.en: Find things on the shelf, queue, pay, and ask the shopkeeper.
blurb.sw: Kutafuta bidhaa, foleni, kulipa na kumuuliza mwenye duka.

blurb.en: Cook ugali, sukuma and chapati, and find your way round a kitchen.
blurb.sw: Kupika ugali, sukuma na chapati, na maneno ya jikoni.

blurb.en: Find a house, talk rent and deposit, and get repairs done.
blurb.sw: Kutafuta nyumba, kodi, amana na marekebisho.

blurb.en: Buy tokens, get through a blackout, refill the gas, and get water.
blurb.sw: Kununua tokeni, stima ikikatika, kujaza gesi na kupata maji.

blurb.en: Laundry, cleaning, and clear, kind instructions at home.
blurb.sw: Kufua, kusafisha na maelekezo mazuri nyumbani.

blurb.en: Fees, uniform, homework and talking to the teacher.
blurb.sw: Karo, sare, kazi ya nyumbani na kuongea na mwalimu.

blurb.en: Lectures, exams, the hostel and friends on campus.
blurb.sw: Mihadhara, mitihani, hosteli na marafiki chuoni.

blurb.en: Meetings, deadlines, the boss, leave and the end of the day.
blurb.sw: Mikutano, muda wa mwisho, bosi, likizo na kumaliza siku.

blurb.en: Customers, stock, credit and the day's takings, from behind the counter.
blurb.sw: Wateja, bidhaa, madeni na mauzo ya siku.

blurb.en: Ask about jobs, the interview, the pay and the first day.
blurb.sw: Kuuliza kazi, usaili, mshahara na siku ya kwanza.

blurb.en: Send, withdraw, pay a bill, and sort out a mistake.
blurb.sw: Kutuma, kutoa, kulipa bili na kurekebisha kosa.

blurb.en: Feeding, sleep, the clinic, play and bedtime.
blurb.sw: Kulisha, usingizi, kliniki, michezo na wakati wa kulala.

blurb.en: Book a seat, carry your luggage, and ask about the journey.
blurb.sw: Kukata tiketi, mizigo na kuuliza kuhusu safari.

en.text: Hello.

sw.note: The reply is Sijambo (I'm well). To an elder say Shikamoo instead (st-0041). To a group: Hamjambo? 'Jambo' alone is what tourists hear; Kenyans say Hujambo or Habari.

en.text: How are you?

sw.note: To a group: Habari zenu? Greet an elder with Shikamoo first.

en.text: I'm fine, thank you. And you?

sw.note: First sentence reuses reviewed amb-0012 exactly.

en.text: Thank you.

sw.note: To a group: Asanteni.

en.text: I don't understand.

sw.note: Sijaelewa = I haven't understood (yet). Both are said every day.

en.text: Please say that again.

sw.note: Adapted from reviewed amb-0027 (Tafadhali sema tena pole pole).

en.text: Slower, please.

sw.note: Pole pole = slowly. (Pole alone = sorry for your trouble.)

en.text: I'm learning Kiswahili.

sw.note: Na- is the everyday short form of nina- (I am ...ing).

en.text: I speak a little Kiswahili.

sw.note: Kuongea is everyday Kenyan; kuzungumza is the more formal word for 'speak'.

en.text: What does that mean?

sw.note: Adapted from reviewed amb-0981 (Neno hilo lina maana gani?).

en.text: How do you say this in Kiswahili?

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0980 exactly. Literally 'this, in Kiswahili, is called how?'.

en.text: Please.

sw.note: Many requests start with Naomba (I ask for) instead: Naomba maji. Use one or the other, not both.

en.text: Excuse me.

sw.note: Also used to say sorry. Add a title to be warm: Samahani, mama. / Samahani, kaka.

en.text: Yes, please.

sw.note: Accepting something offered: naomba (I ask for it), not tafadhali.

en.text: No, thank you.
Do you speak English?
How much is this?

sw.note: Wording from reviewed amb-0065 (How much for this?).

en.text: Where is the toilet?

sw.note: Choo is class 7 (kiko). Choo iko wapi? is also heard; we teach the standard.

en.text: Water, please.

sw.note: Naomba (I ask for) is the polite way to order anything.

en.text: Sorry, I'm still learning.

sw.note: No gender in Swahili: one form for everyone.

en.text: Can you help me, please?
Good morning.

sw.note: Swahili greetings are questions: 'news of the morning?'. The reply is Nzuri or Salama.

en.text: I need a doctor.

sw.note: Alt is reviewed amb-0871.

en.text: Goodbye.

sw.note: To a group: Kwaherini.

en.text: Okay, no problem.

sw.note: Hakuna shida from reviewed amb-0254.

en.text: Good evening.

sw.note: Umeshindaje = how did you spend the day? (reviewed amb-0007 uses it).

en.text: Good night.

sw.note: Wording from reviewed amb-0032. Lala salama = sleep well, said at bedtime.

en.text: Hello, everyone.

sw.note: Group greeting (ham- = you all). The reply is Hatujambo. Hamjambo wote? is also heard.

en.text: Nice to meet you.

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0026 exactly.

en.text: See you later.

sw.note: Adapted from reviewed amb-0030 (Tutaonana baadaye leo).

en.text: See you tomorrow.

sw.note: Adapted from reviewed amb-0029 (Tutaonana kesho asubuhi).

en.text: Have a good day.

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0031 exactly.

en.text: Have a good evening.

sw.note: Same pattern as Uwe na siku njema (amb-0031).

en.text: You too.
Thank you very much.

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0301 (Thank you so much).

en.text: You're welcome.

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0304 exactly. Karibu = the reply to asante.

en.text: Sorry.

sw.note: Samahani = I apologise / excuse me. Pole = sorry for your trouble (someone trips, is sick, had a hard day).

en.text: Peace be upon you.

sw.note: Common on the coast and among Muslims. The Latin spelling of this Arabic greeting varies a lot.

en.text: And peace be upon you.

sw.note: The fixed reply. Spelling varies (Wa alaikum salaam).

en.text: My respects, elder.

sw.note: Respect greeting from a younger person. The elder replies Marahaba. Mzee = respected elder (man); to a woman elder say mama (or bibi for a grandmother). This is a word swap, not grammar.

en.text: Fine. I slept well, thank you.

sw.note: Adapted: Swahili answers the morning greeting with Nzuri (good) instead of saying 'good morning' back.

en.text: Good morning! How did you sleep?

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0004 exactly.

en.text: Good morning! How are you?
Welcome! Come in, come in.

sw.note: Hosts repeat karibu. To a group: Karibuni, karibuni. Ingieni ndani.

en.text: Welcome, please sit down.

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0021 exactly: the set phrase for 'have a seat'. Keti is correct but sounds bookish in Kenya.

en.text: Fine, thank God.

sw.note: Tunamshukuru Mungu (we thank God) is the everyday set phrase, even about yourself.

en.text: I understand.

sw.note: Nimeelewa = I've got it (now).

en.text: Can you write it for me?

sw.note: ku-ni-andiki-a = to write for me.

en.text: Did I say it right?

sw.note: Nimetamka = did I pronounce it.

en.text: Please correct me.

sw.note: Alt = correct me when I get it wrong.

en.text: Speak to me in Kiswahili, please.
Thank you for your patience.

sw.note: Subira (patience) is the coastal favourite; uvumilivu is heard everywhere.

en.text: You speak Kiswahili very well!
Where did you learn Kiswahili?
Yes, that's right.
Almost. Say it again.

sw.note: Umekaribia = you've come close (almost right).

en.text: What's your name?

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0024 exactly.

en.text: Where are you from?

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0166 exactly.

en.text: I live here now.
I'm here for two weeks.
I'm here for work.

alt: Niko hapa kwa ajili ya kazi.

en.text: I came to visit family.
This is my first time here.

sw.text: Hii ni mara yangu ya kwanza kuja hapa.
alt: Ni mara yangu ya kwanza hapa.

en.text: I'm a teacher.

sw.note: Swap in your own job: daktari (doctor), mkulima (farmer), mwanafunzi (student). No gender change.

en.text: I'm married.

sw.note: A man says nimeoa (I have married); a woman says nimeolewa (I have been married). Pattern of reviewed amb-0194. The alt Nina mke is a man's line; a woman says Nina mume.

en.text: I have two children.
I'm thirty years old.
What do you do?

sw.note: Reviewed amb-0174 (What do you do for work?).

en.text: Are you married?

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0193 exactly. Asked of a woman: Umeolewa? The alt Una mke is asked of a man; to a woman: Una mume?

en.text: How long have you been here?
How much are the tomatoes?

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0078 exactly.

en.text: That's too expensive.

sw.note: Adapted from reviewed amb-0476 (Hiyo ni ghali sana kwangu).

en.text: Can you lower the price?

sw.note: Reviewed amb-0083.

en.text: I'll give you eighty.

sw.note: Eighty shillings: a fair offer on one hundred.

en.text: Two for one hundred?
Okay, give me two kilos.

sw.note: At many stalls prices are per pile (fungu): nipe mafungu mawili.

en.text: Just one, please.
I'll take this one.

sw.note: Hii fits most things (class 9). A ki- thing: hiki. An m- thing (mti): huu. A ji-/class 5 thing (tunda, embe): hili.

en.text: Do you have a bigger one?

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0121 exactly.

en.text: I'm just looking, thank you.

sw.note: Adapted from reviewed amb-0137.

en.text: No, that's all, thank you.

sw.note: Ni hayo tu = that's all.

en.text: Do you have change for five hundred?

sw.note: Pattern of reviewed amb-0097. The note people struggle to break in Kenya is often elfu moja (one thousand).

en.text: Can I pay by phone?

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0139 exactly. Most people just say M-Pesa.

en.text: Here you go.

sw.note: Said while handing over money or a thing.

en.text: Keep the change.

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0099 exactly (reviewed at medium confidence).

en.text: Where can I buy water?
One, two, three, four, five.
Six, seven, eight, nine, ten.
Ten, twenty, fifty, one hundred.
Five hundred, one thousand.

sw.note: The Kenyan notes are fifty, one hundred, two hundred, five hundred and one thousand shillings.

en.text: Welcome! What do you need?

sw.note: Adapted: a vegetable seller (mama mboga) says 'what shall I give you?'.

en.text: One kilo is one hundred.

sw.note: One hundred shillings a kilo: a realistic tomato price.

en.text: Okay, how much will you pay?
Ninety, last price.
Anything else?
That's one hundred and eighty.

sw.note: Two kilos at ninety. Na comes before the last number.

en.text: It's fifty.
I don't have change.
Where is the bus station?

sw.note: Reviewed amb-0523 (Where is the bus stop?). For a matatu, people say the stage: Steji ya matatu iko wapi? (steji, from English stage).

en.text: How much to the market?

sw.note: Agree the fare before you get on.

en.text: Take me to the market, please.
Okay, let's go.

sw.note: Adapted from reviewed amb-0412 (Basi twende).

en.text: Go straight, then turn left.

sw.text: Nenda moja kwa moja, halafu pinda kushoto.
alt: Nenda moja kwa moja, halafu kata kushoto.
sw.note: Kata kushoto (cut left) is what many riders say.

en.text: Turn right here.
A little further, please.
Stop here, please.

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0520 exactly. On a matatu, tell the conductor: Nishushe hapa (let me off here). Many Kenyans say Nishukishe.

en.text: Slow down, please.
Is it far?
Is this the way to the hospital?

sw.text: Hii ndiyo njia ya kwenda hospitali?

en.text: How long does it take?
Which matatu goes to the market?

sw.note: Adapted: bus becomes matatu, the shared minibus.

en.text: I'm going to the market.

sw.note: Adapted from reviewed amb-0109 (Nakwenda sokoni asubuhi ya leo). No gender change in Swahili.

en.text: I'm lost.
Where to?

sw.note: A rider's usual question: 'where shall we go?'.

en.text: Which way?
Here?
How about here?
Fifty, please.
Help!

sw.note: Plural: shouted to everyone around.

en.text: Call an ambulance!

sw.note: Gari la wagonjwa is the textbook word; people say ambulensi. To a group: Iteni ambulensi!

en.text: Call the police!
It's an emergency.
Where is the hospital?
Where is the pharmacy?

sw.note: Wording of reviewed amb-0880 (Where is the chemist?). Kenyans call a pharmacy a kemisti.

en.text: Is there a doctor here?
I don't feel well.
I have a headache.

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0866 exactly.

en.text: My stomach hurts.

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0867 exactly.

en.text: I have a fever.

sw.note: Adapted from reviewed amb-0868 (Nina homa kidogo).

en.text: Do you have something for a headache?

sw.text: Una dawa ya maumivu ya kichwa?

en.text: Yes, it's for me.
No, just a headache.
Three times a day, after food?

sw.text: Mara tatu kwa siku, baada ya kula?
alt: Mara tatu kwa siku, baada ya chakula?
sw.note: Say the dose back to check you heard it.

en.text: I'm allergic to penicillin.

sw.note: Mzio is the standard word; aleji is what many Kenyans say. Swap in your real allergy, or skip.

en.text: I lost my phone.
Someone stole my bag.

sw.note: Literally 'I have been stolen-from my bag'. Begi langu (class 5) is standard; begi yangu is also heard.

en.text: Where is the police station?
Please call this number.
Leave me alone!
Hello, can I help you?

sw.note: Adapted: the chemist asks 'what can I help you with?'.

en.text: Is it for you?
Do you have a fever?
Where does it hurt?
Take two, three times a day.

sw.text: Meza mbili, mara tatu kwa siku.
alt: Kunywa mbili, mara tatu kwa siku.
sw.note: Meza = swallow (tablets). Many people say kunywa dawa (drink medicine) for any medicine. Mbili goes with tembe (tablets); with vidonge you will hear viwili.

en.text: Yes, after food.
Tea, please.

sw.note: Kenyan chai comes with milk and sugar already in.

en.text: Coffee, please.
Tea with milk, please.

sw.note: Black tea is chai ya rangi.

en.text: Just a little sugar, please.
No sugar, please.
Just a little, please.
It's delicious.
Thank you, I'm full.
Can I have some more?

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0565 exactly.

en.text: I don't eat meat.
Is it spicy?

sw.note: Pilipili = chilli.

en.text: What's good today?
The bill, please.
Thank you for the food.
Thank you, I will.

sw.note: Adapted: accepting an invitation, Swahili says 'I will come'. After Karibu tena (come again): nitakuja tena or nitarudi.

en.text: What would you like, tea or coffee?
With sugar?

sw.note: Kenyan tea is often served already sweet.

en.text: Would you like something to eat?
Have another cup.
Come again.
Come for tea later.

sw.note: Literally 'come, let's drink tea later'.

en.text: How is your family?

sw.note: Reviewed amb-0010 (How is the family?).

en.text: They're fine, thank God.
This is my wife.
This is my husband.
We came to greet you.

sw.note: To several hosts: Tumekuja kuwasalimia. To an elder, add mzee or mama at the end.

en.text: How is your health, elder?

sw.note: Respect: greet with Shikamoo first. Mzee = elder (man); to a woman elder say mama. A word swap, not grammar.

en.text: The journey was good, thank God.
She's well. She sends her greetings.

sw.note: Hajambo = he or she is well (Swahili has no he/she).

en.text: Do you have children?
Greet your family for me.

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0034 (Say hello to your family for me), same meaning.

en.text: Your home is beautiful.
May God give you long life.

sw.note: A blessing for an elder. Add mzee or mama.

en.text: Yes, we have to go. Thank you for everything.

sw.text: Ndiyo, lazima tuondoke. Asante kwa kila kitu.
alt: Ndiyo, inabidi tuondoke. Asante kwa kila kitu.

en.text: Sit down. How was the journey?

sw.note: Karibu kiti from reviewed amb-0021. To a group: Karibuni viti.

en.text: How is your mother?

sw.note: Alt is reviewed amb-0644.

en.text: Eat, eat! Don't be shy.

sw.note: Hosts insist. Take a little. To a group: Kuleni, kuleni. Msione haya.

en.text: Have some more.

sw.note: To a group: Ongezeni kidogo.

en.text: You're leaving already?

sw.note: Literally: you are leaving this early? To a group: Mnaondoka mapema hivi?

en.text: Can you hear me?

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0591 exactly.

en.text: The network is bad. I'll call you back.

sw.note: Many Kenyans say network for the phone signal.

en.text: My battery is almost dead.

sw.note: Adapted from reviewed amb-0601.

en.text: I'm on my way.

sw.note: From reviewed amb-0041 (Niko njiani, nitafika punde).

en.text: I'll be there in ten minutes.

sw.note: Pattern of reviewed amb-0417.

en.text: I'm running a little late.

sw.note: From reviewed amb-0022 (Samahani, nimechelewa kidogo).

en.text: Are you free tomorrow?

sw.note: Pattern of reviewed amb-0045 (Una nafasi sasa hivi?).

en.text: Let's meet at ten in the morning.

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0415 exactly. Swahili hours count from dawn: ten a.m. is saa nne.

en.text: Let's meet at the bus station.
Where are you now?
Send me a message.
What's your number?
I'm busy right now.

sw.note: No gender change in Swahili.

en.text: Okay, I'll be there.
A little. Can we talk later?
Hello?
Oh, hi! How are you?

sw.note: Adapted: 'Oh, it's you. How are you?'.

en.text: Yes. What time?
Where?
Sorry, I can't hear you.
Okay. See you tomorrow.
The meeting is at ten.

sw.note: Ten o'clock is saa nne in Swahili time.

en.text: Are you busy?
I'm tired.
I'm hungry.

sw.note: From reviewed amb-0284 (Nina njaa kidogo).

en.text: I'm thirsty.
I'm happy to see you.
It's very hot today.

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0832 exactly.

en.text: Yes, it's too hot for me.

sw.note: Adapted: 'the heat is too much'.

en.text: It's cold this morning.

sw.note: Wording of reviewed amb-0836 (It's cool this morning).

en.text: It's going to rain.

sw.note: From reviewed amb-0837 (Nafikiri mvua itanyesha).

en.text: Really?
That's great!
Me too.
Thank God.
God willing.
I like it here.

sw.note: pa- = 'it' for a place: na-pa-penda = I like (this place).

en.text: Don't worry.

sw.note: To a group: Msijali.

en.text: Are you okay?
Get well soon.

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0887 (Please get well soon). Ugua pole = 'be ill gently', the classic wish.

en.text: Congratulations!
How was your weekend?

sw.note: Reviewed amb-0044 (How was the weekend?).

en.text: It was good. I rested.
What are you doing today?
Where are you going today?
Fine, thank God. How was your weekend?
Would you like tea?
Before you go, the water is coming tomorrow morning.

sw.text: Kabla hujaenda, maji yatakuja kesho asubuhi.
sw.note: Maji yatakuja: said when rationed tap water is due.

en.text: Thank you for telling me.
Fill your buckets early.
Okay, I'll get up early.
My grandson is coming from Nairobi today.

sw.text: Mjukuu wangu anakuja kutoka Nairobi leo.

en.text: Come and greet him this evening.
Okay, I'll come by this evening.
If you're going to the market, could you bring me some tomatoes?

sw.note: u-ni-letee = you-me-bring for: a polite request.

en.text: Of course. How many kilos shall I bring you?
One kilo is enough. Here's the money.

sw.text: Kilo moja inatosha. Hizi hapa pesa.
sw.note: Pesa takes the plural agreement: hizi pesa, pesa zangu.

en.text: Okay, I'll be back before twelve.

sw.text: Sawa, nitarudi kabla ya saa sita.
sw.note: Saa sita = twelve o'clock (the Swahili clock starts at dawn).

en.text: Thank you, my child. God bless you.
Yes. Here's your change, three hundred and twenty.

sw.text: Ndiyo. Hii hapa chenji yako, mia tatu na ishirini.

en.text: Thank you. Do you have onions today?
Yes, one pile is fifty.

sw.note: Fungu = a small heap; market sellers price by the fungu.

en.text: Give me two piles.
Shall I add some coriander for you?

sw.note: Sellers often add a free handful (nyongeza) for a good customer.

en.text: That's one hundred. Will you pay by M-Pesa?

sw.text: Ni mia moja. Utalipa kwa M-Pesa?

en.text: Yes, I'll send it to you right now.
Send it to the number written here.
I've sent it. Check your phone.
I've got it, thank you. Come again tomorrow.
Thank you, mama. See you tomorrow.

sw.note: Mama is a polite way to address any grown woman.

en.text: Thank you. Shall I wait and take you back?
No, I'll be a long time.
Then call me when you need me.
Give me your phone, let me save my number.

sw.text: Nipe simu yako, nikuwekee namba yangu.

en.text: Got it. What's your name?
I'm Otieno. I'm here every day.

sw.text: Mimi ni Otieno. Niko hapa kila siku.

en.text: Okay, Otieno. I'll call you in the evening.
If it rains, the fare goes up a little.
All right, see you in the evening.
Thanks, Otieno. Have a good day at work.

sw.note: Kazi njema: a friendly wish to anyone at work.

en.text: Drink lots of water, and sleep early today.

sw.text: Kunywa maji mengi, na ulale mapema leo.

en.text: Okay. And my child has a cough.

sw.text: Sawa. Na mtoto wangu ana kikohozi.

en.text: How old is the child?
Five years old.
This is a children's cough medicine.

sw.text: Hii ni dawa ya kikohozi ya watoto.

en.text: How many times a day should the child take it?

sw.note: a-nywe = should he or she drink: Kiswahili does not mark he or she.

en.text: One spoon, twice a day.

sw.text: Kijiko kimoja, mara mbili kwa siku.

en.text: Morning and evening?
Yes. If the cough gets worse, take the child to hospital.

sw.note: Akizidi kukohoa = if the child coughs more.

en.text: Okay. And how much is this one?

sw.text: Sawa. Na hii ni bei gani?

en.text: It's two hundred. The total is two hundred and fifty.

sw.text: Ni mia mbili. Jumla ni mia mbili na hamsini.

en.text: Here you go. Thanks for your help.

sw.text: Haya, chukua. Asante kwa msaada wako.

en.text: Sorry, I haven't paid yet.
Oh, that's right. It's eighty shillings.
How much are the mandazi?

sw.note: Kenyans say mandazi; the dictionary plural is maandazi.

en.text: One is ten shillings.
Wrap four for me to take away.
Okay. The total is one hundred and twenty.

sw.text: Sawa. Jumla ni mia moja na ishirini.

en.text: Yes, the number is there on the wall.
I see it. I'm sending it now.
Got it. Here are your mandazi.
Thank you. Your tea is really good.

sw.text: Asante. Chai yako ni tamu sana.
sw.note: Tamu (sweet) is how people praise food that tastes good.

en.text: Thank you very much. Have a good day.
Wait, have some tea first.

sw.note: To a group: Ngojeni kwanza mnywe chai.

en.text: Okay, just one cup.
My child will bring you tea right now.

sw.text: Mtoto wangu atakuletea chai sasa hivi.
sw.note: To a group: atawaletea (bring you all).

addressee_pl.text: Mtoto wangu atawaletea chai sasa hivi.

en.text: Thank you, mama, you are very generous.

sw.text: Asante, mama, wewe ni mkarimu sana.

en.text: When you get home, greet your mother for me.

sw.note: Nisalimie X = greet X for me.

en.text: We'll greet her. She'll be very happy.

sw.note: Atasalimika = she will get your greetings: the usual reply.

en.text: I've put aside some oranges for you to take.

sw.note: ku-wekea = to put aside for someone.

en.text: Amen. When will you come back again?
We'll come back next month, God willing.
Bring your children next time.

sw.text: Uje na watoto wako mara ijayo.

addressee_pl.text: Mje na watoto wenu mara ijayo.

en.text: Okay, we'll bring them.
Wait, let me walk you to the road.

sw.note: ku-sindikiza = to walk a guest part of the way.

en.text: Don't trouble yourself, mama. Rest.
All right then. Go in peace.
Hello? Now I can hear you clearly.
I said let's meet at the bus station.

sw.text: Nilisema tukutane kwenye stendi ya basi.

en.text: Which station? There are two.
The big one, near the market.
Okay. Ten o'clock sharp?

sw.note: Saa nne = ten o'clock; kamili = sharp.

en.text: Yes, ten o'clock sharp.
I'll bring my friend, okay?
If you get there before me, wait for me.
Okay. If I'm late, I'll send you a message.
Okay, bye.
Oh, before you leave, is the report ready?

sw.text: Aa, kabla hujaondoka, ripoti iko tayari?

en.text: Not yet. I'll finish it tomorrow morning.
The boss wants it before ten.

sw.text: Bosi anaitaka kabla ya saa nne.
sw.note: Saa nne = ten o'clock.

en.text: Okay, I'll send it at nine.

sw.note: Saa tatu = nine o'clock in the morning.

en.text: Do you need any help?
Yes, send me last month's figures.

sw.text: Ndiyo, nitumie takwimu za mwezi uliopita.

en.text: I'll email them to you tonight.

sw.text: Nitakutumia kwa barua pepe usiku huu.
sw.note: Barua pepe = email; many say email.

en.text: Thank you so much, you've helped me.
No problem. We're in this together.

sw.note: Tuko pamoja: a common Kenyan way to say we stand together.

en.text: I'll buy you tea tomorrow.
Okay then. Good night.
Good night, see you tomorrow.
Where do I get a matatu to Mombasa?
Town, town! Two seats left!

sw.note: Touts shout the route, then how many seats are still empty.

en.text: Going to town? Get in this one.

sw.note: Panda = get on or into any vehicle.

en.text: No, I'm going to Kilifi.
Does this matatu go to Kilifi?
Does it go through Mtwapa?

sw.note: kupitia = to go by way of a place.

en.text: Does it go all the way to Malindi?
No, it ends at Kilifi.

sw.note: inaishia = it ends at: its last stop.

en.text: Which one leaves first?
We're leaving right now.

sw.note: Crews always say this. The matatu leaves when it is full.

en.text: Just one more person, then we go.
Okay. When do we leave?
I'm in a hurry. I'll be late for work.
Where is the driver?
He's coming. He went for tea.
You said we were leaving right away.
It's full. I'll wait for the next one.

sw.note: inayofuata = the one that follows: the next one.

en.text: How much is the fare to town?
Today it's one hundred.
Why has the fare gone up?

sw.note: Mbona = why, with surprise or complaint.

en.text: It's the rain. Everyone wants a matatu.

sw.text: Ni mvua. Kila mtu anataka matatu.

en.text: It was seventy yesterday.
Okay, eighty. Get in.
Everyone else paid seventy.
Is anyone sitting here?
Can I sit by the window?

sw.note: dirisha-ni = at the window: -ni means at or in.

en.text: Someone's by the window. Sit at the back.
Move over a little, please.
Where should I put my bag?

sw.note: ni-li-weke = I-it-put: li stands for begi.

en.text: Put your bag under the seat.

sw.text: Weka begi lako chini ya kiti.

en.text: Is there a charge for luggage?
Add fifty for the luggage.
Careful, there are eggs inside.

sw.note: Pole pole = gently. Pole on its own = sorry for your trouble.

en.text: Fare, please.
I only have a thousand-shilling note.

sw.text: Nina noti ya elfu moja tu.

en.text: Do you take M-Pesa?

sw.note: mna- = you, plural: you mean the whole crew.

en.text: Yes, send it to this number.
I've sent eighty.
Here's the fare for two people.

sw.text: Hii ni nauli ya watu wawili.

en.text: Please pass this money to the conductor.
Wait, I'll give you your change.
You haven't given me my change.

sw.note: hu-ja-ni-pa = you-not yet-me-give.

en.text: I gave you two hundred.
How many minutes to town?
About forty minutes, if there's no traffic.

sw.text: Dakika arobaini hivi, kama hakuna msongamano.
alt: Dakika arobaini hivi, kama hakuna jam.
sw.note: Many Kenyans just say jam: kuna jam.

en.text: Is there traffic on the road today?
We're stuck in traffic.
Is it like this every morning?

sw.note: Huwa = usually is: for what happens again and again.

en.text: Every morning. That's why I leave early.

sw.text: Kila asubuhi. Ndiyo maana naondoka mapema.

en.text: I'm in the matatu. I'll be there soon.

sw.text: Niko kwenye matatu. Nitafika sasa hivi.
sw.note: Nitafika sasa hivi = I'll be there any minute.

en.text: Please turn the music down.
Tell the driver to slow down.

sw.note: a-punguze = that he reduce: after tell, the verb ends in -e.

en.text: Put on your seat belt. There are police ahead.
Can you open the window a little?
Sorry, did I step on you?
Where are you getting off?
I'm getting off at the post office.
Tell me when we reach Mtwapa.

sw.note: tu-ki-fika = we-when-arrive.

en.text: Have we reached Bamburi?
Excuse me, where are we now?
Where do I get off for the hospital?
Post office, is anyone getting off?
Let me off here, please.

sw.note: Many Kenyans say Nishukishe.

en.text: Drop me at the next stop.

sw.note: kituo = a stop. People also say steji, from stage.

en.text: Wait, I haven't got off yet!
What time is the last matatu?

sw.text: Matatu ya mwisho ni saa ngapi?

en.text: The last one leaves at nine at night.

sw.text: Ya mwisho inaondoka saa tatu usiku.
sw.note: saa tatu usiku = nine at night: hours count from dawn.

en.text: Please leave your bag at the counter.

sw.text: Tafadhali acha begi lako kwenye kaunta.
sw.note: Many supermarkets keep shoppers' bags at a counter by the door.

en.text: Excuse me, do you work here?
What are you looking for?
I'm looking for maize flour.

sw.note: Unga wa ngano is wheat flour, for chapati and mandazi.

en.text: Where's the cooking oil?

sw.note: Mafuta is a ma- word, so it takes yako, not iko.

en.text: At the back, near the milk.
Do you sell eggs by the tray?

sw.note: Mna- speaks to the whole shop: you all.

en.text: Could you get me that one up there?

sw.note: ku-ni-shush-ia = to-me-bring down-for.

en.text: Is there a smaller packet?
We only have two-kilo packets.

sw.text: Tuna pakiti za kilo mbili tu.

en.text: Has the sugar run out?
It's finished. Come back tomorrow.
When will it come in?

sw.note: Kuingia is used for new stock arriving: mzigo umeingia.

en.text: Is this on offer?
Buy two, get one free.
Which one is cheaper?

sw.note: Rahisi means cheap in a shop, and easy everywhere else.

en.text: This one has no price on it.
Is this price for one kilo?

sw.text: Bei hii ni ya kilo moja?

en.text: Where do they weigh the fruit?

sw.note: ya-na-pim-wa: the -wa ending means it is done to them (weighed).

en.text: These bananas haven't been weighed.
Is this the queue?
Excuse me, I was here before you.

sw.note: nili-ku-tangulia = I-you-went ahead of.

en.text: Can I go first? I only have one thing.

sw.text: Naweza kutangulia? Nina kitu kimoja tu.

en.text: Go ahead. I have a lot of things.
Cash or M-Pesa?
I'll pay with M-Pesa.
Can I pay by card?
Do you need a bag?
I brought my own bag.

sw.note: Kenya banned plastic bags, so shops sell reusable ones.

en.text: The price on the shelf is different.

sw.text: Bei ya kwenye rafu ni tofauti.

en.text: Please remove the oil. I don't have enough.
The receipt, please.
Take your change and receipt.
The bread is on the receipt twice.

sw.text: Mkate uko mara mbili kwenye risiti.

en.text: Sorry, let me fix that.
This milk has gone bad.

sw.note: Maziwa is a ma- word: maziwa haya, yameharibika.

en.text: I bought it here yesterday.

sw.note: nili-ya-nunua: ya- stands for maziwa (the milk).

en.text: Do you have the receipt?
Can I get my money back?
How's business today?
Bread and half a litre of milk, please.

sw.text: Naomba mkate na maziwa ya nusu lita.
sw.note: Dukas sell milk in half-litre packets.

en.text: The small milk packets are finished.
Okay, I'll take one litre.
Is this bread from today?
Half a kilo of sugar, please.
Half a kilo is one hundred now.

sw.text: Nusu kilo sasa ni mia moja.

en.text: Why has the sugar gone up?

sw.note: Mbona = why, with a touch of surprise or complaint.

en.text: We buy it at a high price too.

sw.text: Hata sisi tunainunua kwa bei ghali.

en.text: Give me two eggs, please.

sw.note: Mayai (eggs) is a ma- word, so two is mawili.

en.text: That's two hundred and ninety altogether.

sw.text: Jumla ni mia mbili na tisini.

en.text: I only have two hundred on M-Pesa.

sw.text: Nina mia mbili tu kwenye M-Pesa.

en.text: No problem. I'll write it in my book.

sw.text: Hakuna shida, nitaandika kwenye daftari langu.
sw.note: Many dukas keep a daftari of what regulars owe.

en.text: What's the till number?

sw.note: A till is a shop's own number for M-Pesa payments.

en.text: Pay to the till number on the wall.

sw.text: Lipa kwa namba ya till iliyo ukutani.

en.text: I've paid. Here's the message.
I haven't got the message yet.

sw.note: si-ja-pata: -ja- means 'not yet'.

en.text: Let's wait a little.
Okay, I've got it now.

sw.note: nime-u-pata: u- stands for ujumbe (the message).

en.text: How much do I owe you?

sw.note: Ku-dai = to be owed: u-na-ni-dai, you are owed by me.

en.text: You owe me ninety.
Okay, I'll bring it tomorrow morning.

sw.note: nita-zi-leta: zi- stands for pesa (the money).

en.text: Write it down for me. I'll pay tomorrow.
Sorry, I don't give credit.
I've come to pay what I owe.
No, I'll leave it, thank you.
What time do you close?
We close at ten at night.

sw.note: Swahili hours count from dawn: saa nne usiku is ten at night.

en.text: Are you open on Sundays?
Can I help you cook?

sw.note: ni-ku-saidi-e = shall I help you.

en.text: What are we cooking tonight?
Let's cook ugali and sukuma.

sw.note: Sukuma wiki means 'push the week': cheap greens that last till payday.

en.text: Should I cook rice too?

sw.note: Mchele is raw rice; wali is cooked rice.

en.text: How many people are eating?
We've run out of cooking oil.
What should I do first?
Teach me, please.
I don't know how to make chapati.
Can you show me how to make ugali?

sw.text: Unaweza kunionyesha jinsi ya kusonga ugali?
sw.note: kusonga ugali: the verb for making ugali, turning it with a wooden spoon.

en.text: Is the water boiling?

sw.note: ya- agrees with maji: maji yamechemka.

en.text: How much flour do I add?
Your turn. My arm is tired.
The ugali is too soft.
Is the ugali ready?

sw.note: ugali is a u- word: ugali umeiva, ugali uko tayari.

en.text: Like this?
Is the dough soft now?

sw.note: unga is flour, and also the dough.

en.text: How many chapatis should I make?
Should I turn it over now?

sw.note: ni-i-geuz-e: the second i stands for the chapati.

en.text: These chapatis are so soft.
Shall I chop the sukuma?

sw.note: katakata = cut into small pieces; ni-katekat-e = shall I chop.

en.text: Do you put tomatoes in the sukuma?
Should I fry the onions first?
Is this enough oil?

sw.note: mafuta is a ma- word: mafuta haya yanatosha.

en.text: The onions are making me cry.

sw.note: kuliza = to make someone cry, from kulia, to cry.

en.text: The onions are burning.
The gas has run out, and the food isn't cooked yet.

sw.text: Gesi imeisha, na chakula bado hakijaiva.
sw.note: bado + a -ja- verb = not yet: hakijaiva, it isn't cooked yet.

en.text: Where are the matches?

sw.note: kiberiti is one box of matches, so kiko.

en.text: The charcoal hasn't caught fire yet.
Where are the spices?
This knife is blunt.
Pass me the salt, please.
Where do I throw the peelings?
The food smells so good.

sw.note: kunukia = to smell good; kunuka usually means to stink.

en.text: Here, taste this.

sw.note: Hebu softens a request: go on, let's see.

en.text: Is there enough salt?
It's too salty.

sw.note: -zidi = be too much: chumvi imezidi, pilipili imezidi.

en.text: What else do we put in?
Shall I serve the food?

sw.note: kupakua = to dish food out of the pot.

en.text: The food will be ready at seven.

sw.text: Chakula kitakuwa tayari saa moja usiku.
sw.note: Seven in the evening is saa moja usiku: the first hour of night.

en.text: Let's warm up yesterday's food.

sw.note: kupasha moto = to warm up (literally, to make hot).

en.text: Let me wash the dishes.

sw.note: vyombo = dishes, pots and cutlery together.

en.text: No, let me help you.
Where do I put the plates?

sw.note: zi = them, for sahani: ni-zi-wek-e.

en.text: Put the leftovers in the fridge.
Thank you for teaching me.
My mother taught me.
Come, let's cook together.
Chapati and sukuma. Do you know how to make chapati?

sw.text: Chapati na sukuma. Unajua kupika chapati?

en.text: Don't worry, I'll show you.
Add the water a little at a time.

sw.note: kidogo kidogo = little by little.

en.text: Yes. Now knead the dough well.
Good. Now let's cook the sukuma.
Yes, start with the onions.
That's enough. Turn the heat down a little.

sw.note: Yanatosha agrees with mafuta (oil).

en.text: No problem, we'll use the charcoal jiko.

sw.text: Hakuna shida, tutatumia jiko la makaa.
sw.note: jiko is the stove; jikoni is the kitchen.

en.text: It's in the cupboard.

sw.note: Kiko agrees with kiberiti, the matchbox.

en.text: The food is ready. Wash your hands.

sw.note: kunawa = to wash your hands or face; kuosha is for other things.

en.text: You cooked really well.
Who taught you to cook?
Leave the dishes, you're a guest.
Wait until the oil is hot.
Turn it over, it's burning.

sw.note: The i in igeuze and inaungua stands for the chapati.

en.text: Make about ten.
Go ahead, serve yourself.

sw.note: ji- = yourself: ji-pakuli-e, dish out for yourself.

en.text: Add a little more flour.
Keep stirring.

sw.note: kusonga = to stir and press ugali until it's firm.

en.text: The water's boiling. Add the flour.
Are there any houses to rent here?

sw.note: kupanga = to rent as a tenant; kupangisha = to let out.

en.text: Is the landlord in?

sw.note: mwenye nyumba = landlord, literally the owner of the house.

en.text: I'm looking for a bedsitter near here.

sw.note: Kenyans use the English word bedsitter: one room with its own toilet.

en.text: I want a house with one bedroom.

sw.text: Nataka nyumba yenye chumba kimoja cha kulala.
sw.note: chumba cha kulala = bedroom, literally a room for sleeping.

en.text: Is the house still available?

sw.note: iko wazi = it is open; for a house, it is vacant.

en.text: Yes, there's just one bedsitter left.
Can I see it now?

sw.note: ku-i-ona = to-it-see; i- stands for nyumba.

en.text: Okay, follow me.

sw.note: ni- here means me: nifuate = follow me.

en.text: How much is the rent a month?

sw.text: Kodi ni shilingi ngapi kwa mwezi?
alt: Kodi ni pesa ngapi kwa mwezi?
sw.note: kodi = rent; it also means tax.

en.text: It's eight thousand a month.

sw.note: elfu nane = eight thousand; elfu comes first.

en.text: Is seven thousand possible?
This room is small for me.

sw.note: chumba takes ki-: chumba hiki ni kidogo.

en.text: Does the rent include water?

sw.note: pamoja na = together with; here, including.

en.text: No, water has its own meter.

sw.note: maji takes ya-: maji yana = water has.

en.text: Does the water come every day?
Water comes three days a week.

sw.text: Maji huja siku tatu kwa wiki.
sw.note: hu-ja = usually comes; hu- is for regular habits.

en.text: Is there a water tank?

sw.note: tanki takes la: tanki la maji.

en.text: Yes, there's a big tank on the roof.

sw.text: Ndiyo, kuna tanki kubwa juu ya paa.

en.text: Is the power on tokens?

sw.note: tokeni = prepaid electricity you buy on M-Pesa.

en.text: Yes, you'll buy your own tokens.
Is it safe around here at night?
Is there a guard at night?

sw.note: Many people call a guard askari.

en.text: What time is the gate locked?

sw.note: hu-fungwa = is usually locked.

en.text: The gate is locked at ten at night.

sw.note: Swahili time counts from dawn: saa nne usiku is ten at night.

en.text: How many months' rent is the deposit?

sw.note: amana = deposit; many people just say deposit.

en.text: The deposit is two months' rent.

sw.text: Amana ni kodi ya miezi miwili.
sw.note: miezi takes mi-: miezi miwili = two months.

en.text: Can I pay the deposit in two instalments?

sw.text: Naweza kulipa amana kwa awamu mbili?
sw.note: awamu = a round, an instalment.

en.text: Okay, but pay half now.
Viewing a house costs five hundred shillings.

sw.text: Kuona nyumba ni shilingi mia tano.
sw.note: A house agent is a dalali; many charge a viewing fee.

en.text: Okay, I'll take it.

sw.note: ni-ta-i-chukua = I-will-it-take; i- is for nyumba.

en.text: I'll send the money on M-Pesa right now.

sw.text: Nitatuma pesa kwa M-Pesa sasa hivi.

en.text: I've received it. Here's your receipt.

sw.note: Hii hapa = here it is, when handing something over.

en.text: Bring a copy of your ID.

sw.note: kitambulisho = ID card; it takes ch-: kitambulisho chako.

en.text: Please give me a copy of the agreement.

sw.note: mkataba = contract or agreement.

en.text: When can I move in?

sw.note: kuhamia = to move in; kuhama = to move out.

en.text: You can move in on Saturday.
Okay, see you on Saturday.

sw.note: tu-ta-onana = we-will-see each other.

en.text: Who do I get the keys from?

sw.note: ufunguo = a key; funguo = keys.

en.text: Who do I call if something breaks?

sw.note: ki-ki-haribika = if it breaks; -ki- here means if.

en.text: Can I paint the walls?

sw.note: kupaka rangi = to paint; ukuta = wall, kuta = walls.

en.text: Rent is paid at the start of the month.

sw.note: mwanzoni mwa mwezi = at the start of the month.

en.text: I've sent you the rent on M-Pesa.

sw.note: ni-me-ku-tumia = I-have-you-sent to.

en.text: Please give me a receipt for the rent.
Have you paid this month's rent?
The rent will be a little late this month.
Please give me three more days.

sw.note: u-ni-pe = you-me-give; after Naomba the verb ends in -e.

en.text: The rent is going up next month.

sw.note: mwezi ujao = the coming month, next month.

en.text: Why is the rent going up?

sw.note: Mbona = why, with surprise.

en.text: That's more than I can afford.

sw.note: uwezo = ability, what you can manage.

en.text: The kitchen tap is leaking.

sw.note: mfereji = tap; it takes u-: mfereji unavuja.

en.text: Which tap is leaking?

sw.note: upi = which one, for u- nouns like mfereji.

en.text: There's been no water since morning.
The toilet is blocked.

sw.note: choo takes ki-: ki-me-ziba = it has blocked.

en.text: The roof leaks when it rains.

sw.note: i-ki-nyesha = when it rains; -ki- means when.

en.text: The door lock is broken.

sw.note: kufuli = lock or padlock; kitasa = a door lock.

en.text: The bathroom bulb has blown.

sw.note: kuungua = to burn; a blown bulb has burnt.

en.text: Please send a plumber.

sw.note: fundi wa mabomba = plumber, literally repairman of pipes.

en.text: I'll send the plumber tomorrow.

sw.note: ni-ta-m-tuma = I-will-him-send.

en.text: When will he come?

sw.note: a- is he or she: atakuja = he or she will come.

en.text: I've waited a whole week.

sw.note: wiki takes n-: wiki nzima = a whole week.

en.text: Shall I fix it myself, then deduct the cost from the rent?

sw.text: Nitengeneze mwenyewe, halafu nikate gharama kwenye kodi?
sw.note: Nitengeneze, nikate: the -e ending asks shall I.

en.text: I'm giving you one month's notice.

sw.note: na-ku-pa = I-you-give.

en.text: Before you move out, give me one month's notice.

sw.text: Kabla ya kuhama, nipe notisi ya mwezi mmoja.

en.text: I'm moving out at the end of the month.
When will I get my deposit back?

sw.note: ni-ta-rudishiwa = I-will-be-given-back.

en.text: I've left the house clean.
You'll pay for the broken window.

sw.note: li-li-lo-vunjika = it-past-which-broke; dirisha takes li-.

en.text: The window was already broken when I moved in.

sw.note: ni-li-po-hamia = I-past-when-moved in.

en.text: The power's gone off.

sw.note: kukatika = to be cut; for power, to go off.

en.text: Hello, may I come in?

sw.note: Call Hodi at a door; the answer is Karibu.

en.text: Come in.
Do you have power at your place?

sw.note: kwako = at your place; kwangu = at my place.

en.text: No, the whole estate is dark.

sw.note: mtaa takes u-: mtaa mzima uko gizani.

en.text: I heard the transformer blew.
Let me call KPLC.

sw.note: ni-wa-pigie = I-them-call; KPLC is treated as people.

en.text: What did they say?
They say the power will be back by nine tonight.

sw.text: Wanasema stima itarudi kufikia saa tatu usiku.
sw.note: saa tatu usiku = nine at night; the clock counts from dawn.

en.text: Do you have a spare candle?

sw.note: wa ziada = extra, spare.

en.text: Yes, take this one.

sw.note: huu = this, for mshumaa and other m-/mi- nouns.

en.text: Where are the candles?

sw.note: mshumaa = candle; mishumaa = candles, which take i-.

en.text: Can I charge my phone at your place?
Have you cooked dinner yet?

sw.note: u-me-sha-pika = you-have-already-cooked.

en.text: My gas ran out last night.

sw.note: A finished event with a time takes -li-: iliisha.

en.text: Come and cook at my place.
Thank you, you're very kind.

sw.note: Una roho nzuri = you have a good heart.

en.text: Tomorrow I'll show you where to refill gas.

sw.text: Kesho nitakuonyesha mahali pa kujaza gesi.
sw.note: mahali takes pa-: mahali pa kujaza gesi.

en.text: How much does a six-kilo refill cost?

sw.text: Kujaza kilo sita ni shilingi ngapi?

en.text: About one thousand three hundred.

sw.text: Kama elfu moja na mia tatu.
sw.note: elfu moja na mia tatu = one thousand three hundred.

en.text: Everything has gone up in price these days.

sw.text: Kila kitu kimepanda bei siku hizi.
sw.note: kupanda bei = to go up in price.

en.text: Oh, the power's back.
Wait a bit before switching on the fridge.

sw.text: Subiri kidogo kabla ya kuwasha friji.

en.text: Okay, I'll switch it on in ten minutes.

sw.text: Sawa, nitaiwasha baada ya dakika kumi.
sw.note: ni-ta-i-washa = I-will-it-switch on; friji takes i-.

en.text: Okay, let me go home. Good night.

sw.text: Haya, ngoja nirudi nyumbani. Usiku mwema.

en.text: Unplug the TV.

sw.note: runinga = TV; many people just say TV.

en.text: When will the power come back?
My power has been off since this morning.
What's your meter number?

sw.text: Namba ya mita yako ni ngapi?
sw.note: A number is asked with ngapi: namba ni ngapi?

en.text: Shall I read you the meter number?

sw.note: ni-ku-somee = shall I-you-read for.

en.text: Our technicians are on the way.
The power will be off until five in the evening.

sw.text: Stima itazimwa mpaka saa kumi na moja jioni.
sw.note: saa kumi na moja jioni = five in the evening.

en.text: A power line has fallen on the road.
I need to buy tokens.

sw.note: Many people say kununua stima, to buy power.

en.text: How do I buy tokens on M-Pesa?

sw.note: -je on a verb asks how: nanunua-je = how do I buy.

en.text: What's the KPLC paybill number?

sw.text: Paybill ya KPLC ni namba gani?
alt: Namba ya paybill ya KPLC ni ngapi?
sw.note: Kenyans say paybill, the M-Pesa word, as it is.

en.text: I've bought tokens for one thousand shillings.

sw.text: Nimenunua tokeni za shilingi elfu moja.

en.text: I've paid, but I haven't got the token.

sw.note: si-ja-pata = I-not yet-got.

en.text: How do I put the token into the meter?
The meter is rejecting the token.
How many units are left?

sw.note: yuniti = units on the meter; they take zi-.

en.text: We're using a lot of power this month.

sw.text: Tunatumia stima nyingi sana mwezi huu.

en.text: Switch off the lights that aren't in use.

sw.note: zi-si-zo-tumika = that-are-not-being-used; taa takes zi-.

en.text: At home we use solar.

sw.note: sola = solar power, solar panels.

en.text: Please refill this cylinder for me.

sw.note: mtungi = a gas cylinder; also a water jerrican.

en.text: Six kilos or thirteen?

sw.text: Kilo sita au kumi na tatu?
sw.note: kumi na tatu = ten and three, thirteen.

en.text: Thirteen kilos is three thousand.

sw.text: Kilo kumi na tatu ni elfu tatu.

en.text: Do you deliver to the house?

sw.note: Mna- = you plural; you ask the shop as a group.

en.text: Bring the empty cylinder.

sw.note: mtupu = empty; it agrees with mtungi.

en.text: I'll bring it to you in thirty minutes.

sw.note: ni-ta-ku-letea = I-will-you-bring to.

en.text: I think the gas is leaking.
Let me check if it's leaking.
Turn off the gas at the cylinder.

sw.note: kufunga = to close; for gas, to turn off.

en.text: Open the windows, quickly.
Don't switch on any lights.

sw.note: u-si-washe = you-don't-switch on; the don't form ends in -e.

en.text: The taps aren't running.

sw.note: mifereji takes i-: haitoi = they don't give out.

en.text: Which are the water rationing days?

sw.text: Siku za mgao wa maji ni zipi?
sw.note: mgao = rationing, a sharing out.

en.text: Water comes on Tuesdays and Fridays.

sw.note: hu-ja = usually comes.

en.text: Let's fill the tank tonight.

sw.note: leo usiku = tonight, literally today at night.

en.text: There's no water left in the tank.

sw.note: tanki takes li-: ha-li-na = it has no.

en.text: How much is one jerrican?
A jerrican is thirty shillings.
How many jerricans do you want?

sw.note: mingapi agrees with mitungi.

en.text: Bring me ten jerricans.

sw.note: ni-let-ee = bring for me.

en.text: Pour it into the tank.

sw.note: ya- = it, for maji: ya-mimin-e.

en.text: Is this drinking water?

sw.note: haya here means these, for maji.

en.text: Boil the water first.
The water bill is very high this month.

sw.text: Bili ya maji iko juu sana mwezi huu.
alt: Bili ya maji imepanda sana mwezi huu.

en.text: Today is laundry day.

sw.text: Leo ni siku ya kufua nguo.
sw.note: kufua = wash clothes; kuosha = wash dishes or a car.

en.text: Here's the plan for this week.

sw.text: Mpango wa wiki hii ni huu.

en.text: On Wednesday, please clean the windows.

sw.note: Juma + tano: Wednesday is day five, counting from Saturday.

en.text: We're having visitors on Saturday.

sw.note: kuwa na = to have: tutakuwa na = we will have.

en.text: Please clean the guest room.
You don't need to cook today.
What time will you come tomorrow?

sw.note: saa ngapi = what time (literally, how many hours).

en.text: Can you come at seven instead?

sw.text: Unaweza kuja saa moja badala yake?
sw.note: Seven in the morning is saa moja: the first hour after dawn.

en.text: Don't wash the white clothes with the coloured ones.

sw.text: Usifue nguo nyeupe pamoja na za rangi.
sw.note: za rangi = the coloured ones: za agrees with nguo.

en.text: Please hang the clothes in the sun.

sw.note: kuanika = hang out to dry; kuanua = bring in off the line.

en.text: Yes, bring them in quickly.

sw.note: zi = them, for nguo: zi-anu-e.

en.text: Then hang them up inside.
Yes, and fold them nicely.
Put them in the wardrobe.

sw.note: -ni = in: kabati, kabatini.

en.text: Please iron the children's uniforms.

sw.text: Tafadhali piga pasi sare za watoto.
sw.note: kupiga pasi = to iron (literally, to hit with the iron).

en.text: Okay, you'll do the ironing tomorrow.
Please sweep outside first.
Mop the floor after sweeping.

sw.note: kupiga deki = to mop the floor.

en.text: Please start in the kitchen.
Please clean the toilet and the bathroom.
When you get a moment, please make the beds.

sw.note: u-ki-pata = if or when you get.

en.text: Please wash last night's dishes.

sw.text: Naomba uoshe vyombo vya jana usiku.
sw.note: Naomba + a verb in -e is a polite request: naomba uoshe.

en.text: Please take the rubbish out.
The rubbish truck comes every Thursday.

sw.text: Gari la taka huja kila Alhamisi.
sw.note: hu- = usually: huja = it comes, as a rule.

en.text: Leave the rubbish bag at the gate.
Take this money and buy more at the shop.

sw.text: Chukua pesa hii ununue nyingine dukani.
sw.note: u-nunu-e: the second verb of a request takes -e.

en.text: Here's your salary for this month.

sw.text: Huu hapa mshahara wako wa mwezi huu.
sw.note: Huu hapa = here it is; huu agrees with mshahara.

en.text: I'll pay you at the end of the month.
I've sent your salary by M-Pesa.
Has the money come through?

sw.note: pesa takes zi- here: pesa zimeingia.

en.text: Sorry, your salary is late this month.

sw.text: Samahani, mshahara wako umechelewa mwezi huu.

en.text: I'll pay you on Friday.
Take this for your fare.

sw.note: nauli = the fare for a matatu, bus or boda.

en.text: You can take Sunday off.
Is everything okay at home?
I'm so sorry. Go and see her.

sw.note: Pole is for someone's trouble; samahani is for your own mistake.

en.text: Don't worry. Mind the broken pieces.
Yes, but finish the ironing first.

sw.text: Ndiyo, lakini maliza kupiga pasi kwanza.

en.text: Thank you, the house is sparkling.
You've worked hard today. Rest now.

sw.text: Umefanya kazi sana leo. Pumzika sasa.

en.text: Thank you for all your help.
Don't open the gate for someone you don't know.

sw.note: u-si-ye-m-jua = whom you don't know.

en.text: Lock the door when you go out.
Have a safe journey.
Whose turn is it to clean?
Let's share the work.

sw.note: tu-gawan-e = let's divide it among ourselves.

en.text: You sweep, and I'll wash the dishes.
Please wash your dishes.
What should I do today?
Where should I start?

sw.note: anzia = start from: nianzie wapi?

en.text: Okay. What about these coloured ones?
It's going to rain. Should I bring the washing in?
The clothes aren't dry yet.
Should I iron these too?

sw.note: nazo = these too (na + zo, for nguo).

en.text: The power's off, so I can't iron.

sw.note: stima = electricity in Kenya; umeme also works.

en.text: I've finished. Is there anything else?
I'd like Saturday off, please.

sw.note: Naomba + a verb in -e: a polite way to ask.

en.text: My mother is sick back home.

sw.note: nyumbani often means your home village, not your house in town.

en.text: Thank you. I'll be back on Monday.
Thank you so much. God bless you.
We've run out of soap.
I've broken a glass. I'm sorry.
Can I leave early today?
I'll come at eight in the morning.

sw.note: Eight in the morning is saa mbili: the second hour after dawn.

en.text: Where do I put the clean clothes?
Where do you keep the broom?

sw.note: mna-u-weka: you all keep it; u stands for ufagio.

en.text: Could you pay me early this month?
Careful, the floor is still wet.
How are you, teacher?
Thank you. I've come for my son's report.

sw.text: Asante. Nimekuja kuchukua ripoti ya mwanangu.
alt: Asante. Nimekuja kuchukua ripoti ya mtoto wangu.
sw.note: mwanangu = my child (mwana wangu): a son or a daughter.

en.text: Can I see the head teacher?
The head teacher is in a meeting. Please wait.

sw.text: Mwalimu mkuu yuko kwenye mkutano. Tafadhali subiri.
alt: Mwalimu mkuu yuko mkutanoni. Tafadhali ngoja.

en.text: I'm his parent.
Is there a place for a new pupil?
I want to enrol my child here.

sw.note: ku-mw-andikisha = to get him or her registered (andika = write).

en.text: Bring her birth certificate and two passport photos.

sw.text: Leta cheti chake cha kuzaliwa na picha mbili za pasipoti.

en.text: Which grade is she going into?

sw.note: darasa la ngapi? = which class (class of how many)?

en.text: She's going into Grade Four.
How much are the fees this term?

sw.text: Karo ya muhula huu ni shilingi ngapi?
sw.note: karo = school fees; muhula = school term.

en.text: It's twenty thousand shillings a term.

sw.text: Ni shilingi elfu ishirini kwa muhula.
sw.note: elfu ishirini = twenty thousand: elfu (thousand) comes first.

en.text: Can I pay her fees in two instalments?

sw.text: Naweza kulipa karo yake kwa awamu mbili?
sw.note: kwa awamu mbili = in two instalments (in two rounds).

en.text: How are the fees paid?

sw.note: -je on a verb asks how: inalipwa-je = it is paid how?

en.text: You can pay through the bank or M-Pesa.

sw.text: Unaweza kulipa kupitia benki au M-Pesa.

en.text: I've paid half the fees.
I'll finish paying at the end of the month.
Another thing, you still owe three thousand shillings.

sw.text: Jambo lingine, bado unadaiwa shilingi elfu tatu.
sw.note: u-na-dai-wa = you are being claimed from: you owe.

en.text: Please give me until Friday.

sw.note: Naomba unipe = please give me (I ask that you give me).

en.text: Okay. I'll pay on Friday.
My child was sent home for fees yesterday.

sw.text: Jana mwanangu alirudishwa nyumbani kwa sababu ya karo.
sw.note: a-li-rudish-wa = he or she was sent back.

en.text: The fees went up this term.
Where can I get the school uniform?

alt: Naweza kununua sare ya shule wapi?
sw.note: sare = uniform; you will also hear the English word.

en.text: Which books does she need this term?
How is my child doing?

sw.note: anaendelea-je = how is he or she getting on?

en.text: He's doing well in most subjects.
Which subject is giving him trouble?

sw.note: li-na-lo-m-pa = that gives him (somo takes li- words).

en.text: He's a bit behind in English.
How can I help him at home?

sw.note: ni-m-saidie-je = how should I help him?

en.text: He needs to read more at home.
I'll read with him every evening.

sw.note: naye = with him or her (na + yeye).

en.text: Please sign his book every day.

sw.text: Tafadhali weka sahihi kwenye daftari lake kila siku.

en.text: There's so much homework these days.

sw.text: Siku hizi kazi ya nyumbani ni nyingi sana.

en.text: Even I don't understand this homework.

sw.text: Hata mimi sielewi kazi hii ya nyumbani.

en.text: He didn't bring his homework.

sw.note: ha-ku-leta = he or she did not bring.

en.text: Sorry, he'll bring it tomorrow.

sw.note: a-ta-i-leta: i- stands for kazi (the homework).

en.text: Your child talks a lot in class.

sw.note: mwanao = your child (mwana wako).

en.text: I'm sorry. I'll talk to him.
My child is being bullied by another child.

sw.note: kuonewa = to be picked on or bullied.

en.text: We'll deal with it today.

sw.note: tu-ta-li-shughulikia: li- stands for jambo (the matter).

en.text: Is she getting along with the other children?

sw.note: kuelewana = to get along (understand each other).

en.text: My child is sick today.
He won't come to school today.

sw.note: ha-ta-ku-ja: kuja keeps its ku- after -ta-.

en.text: She missed school yesterday because she was sick.

sw.text: Jana hakuja shuleni kwa sababu alikuwa mgonjwa.

en.text: Here's the doctor's note.
Please give him his medicine at lunchtime.

sw.text: Tafadhali mpe dawa yake wakati wa chakula cha mchana.

en.text: Your child has a fever. Please come for him.

sw.text: Mtoto wako ana homa. Tafadhali njoo umchukue.

en.text: I'm coming right now.
I'll pick her up at four.

sw.note: saa kumi = four o'clock: hours count from dawn.

en.text: My sister will pick him up today.
Who is picking her up today?
What time does the school van come?

sw.text: Gari la shule linakuja saa ngapi?
sw.note: gari takes li- words: gari la shule linakuja.

en.text: The van comes at half past six in the morning.

sw.text: Gari linakuja saa kumi na mbili na nusu asubuhi.
sw.note: saa kumi na mbili asubuhi = six in the morning.

en.text: The school van didn't come this morning.

sw.text: Gari la shule halikuja leo asubuhi.

en.text: How much is the school van a month?

sw.text: Gari la shule ni shilingi ngapi kwa mwezi?

en.text: What time is the parents' meeting?

sw.text: Mkutano wa wazazi ni saa ngapi?

en.text: The parents' meeting is on Saturday at nine in the morning.

sw.text: Mkutano wa wazazi ni Jumamosi saa tatu asubuhi.
sw.note: saa tatu asubuhi = nine in the morning.

en.text: I can't come to the meeting. I'll be at work.

sw.text: Sitaweza kuja kwenye mkutano. Nitakuwa kazini.

en.text: When do the exams start?
The exams start next Monday.
Okay, but finish paying before the exams.

sw.text: Sawa, lakini maliza kulipa kabla ya mitihani.

en.text: How did she do in the exams?
She passed all her exams.

sw.note: kufaulu = to pass an exam.

en.text: When do you close for the holidays?

sw.note: kufunga shule = to close school for the holidays.

en.text: Which class is your child in?

sw.text: Mtoto wako yuko darasa la ngapi?

en.text: Does your child take the school van?

sw.text: Mtoto wako anatumia gari la shule?

en.text: Did you get the message from the school?
Thank you for coming.
What time does the lecture start?
Sorry I'm late. May I come in?
The lecturer hasn't come yet.

sw.note: ha-ja-fika = he has not yet arrived.

en.text: I didn't understand today's lecture.

sw.note: si-ku-elewa = I-did not-understand.

en.text: Could you explain this part again?
I didn't come to class yesterday. I was sick.
Can I come to your office tomorrow?
Will this come up in the exam?
Which topics should we read for the exam?

sw.text: Tusome mada gani kwa ajili ya mtihani?

en.text: Is the exam timetable out?
Not yet. When is our first exam?

sw.text: Bado. Mtihani wetu wa kwanza ni lini?

en.text: I'm nervous about tomorrow's exam.

sw.text: Nina wasiwasi kuhusu mtihani wa kesho.
sw.note: Nina wasiwasi = I have worry: feelings often use 'have'.

en.text: How was the exam?
It was hard, but I tried.

sw.note: u-likuwa and m-gumu agree with mtihani (the exam).

en.text: Are the results out?
I passed all my exams.
I have to resit one exam.

sw.note: Kenyan students call a resit a supp, short for supplementary.

en.text: When do we hand in the assignment?

sw.note: ku-wasilisha = to hand in or present work.

en.text: I haven't finished my assignment yet.

sw.note: si-ja-maliza = I-not yet-finish.

en.text: Can I hand it in on Monday?

sw.note: ku-i-wasilisha: -i- is 'it', agreeing with kazi.

en.text: Then I'll finish it tomorrow.
Where can I find this book?

sw.note: ni-ta-ki-pata: -ki- is 'it', agreeing with kitabu.

en.text: I'd like to borrow this book.
Is this seat taken?

sw.note: Literally: does this seat have a person?

en.text: Which group are you in?
I'll write the introduction.
Send me your part tonight.
Can I borrow your notes? Mine aren't complete.

sw.text: Naweza kuazima maelezo yako? Yangu hayajakamilika.
alt: Naomba kuazima maelezo yako. Yangu hayajakamilika.
sw.note: Yangu and ha-ya-ja-kamilika agree with maelezo (notes).

en.text: I'll bring your notes back tomorrow morning.

sw.note: ni-ta-ku-rudishia = I-will-you-return to.

en.text: Is there space in the hostel?
How much is a room per semester?

sw.text: Chumba ni bei gani kwa muhula?
sw.note: muhula = a term or semester.

en.text: There's been no water in the bathroom since morning.
The room next door is very noisy at night.

sw.text: Chumba cha jirani kina kelele sana usiku.

en.text: I lost my room key.
I haven't paid this semester's fees yet.

sw.text: Bado sijalipa karo ya muhula huu.
sw.note: karo = school or college fees in Kenya.

en.text: My loan hasn't come in yet.

sw.note: Money 'enters' (ku-ingia) your account.

en.text: Can I pay the fees in instalments?

sw.note: kwa awamu = in parts, in instalments.

en.text: I'm broke until the loan comes.
Can you lend me two hundred until Friday?

sw.text: Unaweza kunikopesha mia mbili mpaka Ijumaa?
sw.note: ku-kopesha = to lend money; ku-kopa = to borrow it.

en.text: What are you studying?

sw.note: ku-somea = to study for a course or career.

en.text: I'm studying nursing.
Let's go and eat at the canteen.

sw.note: tu-ka-le: -ka- adds 'go and' to 'let us eat'.

en.text: When does the semester end?
Good luck in the exam.
When is graduation?

sw.note: mahafali = the graduation ceremony.

en.text: My parents are coming to my graduation.

sw.text: Wazazi wangu watakuja kwenye mahafali yangu.

en.text: Let's study together later.
Monday? I'm not ready at all.

sw.note: hata kidogo = not even a little: not at all.

en.text: I'll ask my parents to help me.

sw.note: wa-ni-saidie = that they help me.

en.text: Did you understand anything?
Me neither. He taught too fast.
Okay. At the library at four?

sw.note: Four in the afternoon is saa kumi jioni.

en.text: Have you seen the exam timetable?

sw.note: u-me-i-ona: -i- points ahead to ratiba.

en.text: It's on Monday, at eight in the morning.
Don't worry, we still have five days.
The lecturer said to read the first five chapters.

sw.text: Mhadhiri alisema tusome sura tano za kwanza.

en.text: Sure, but bring them back tomorrow.
How far have you got with the assignment?

sw.note: Literally: where have you reached with the work?

en.text: The deadline is Friday at twelve noon.

sw.text: Mwisho wa kuwasilisha ni Ijumaa saa sita mchana.

en.text: What about the fees? Have you paid?

sw.note: Na ... je? = what about ...?

en.text: You can't sit the exam until you pay all the fees.

sw.text: Huwezi kufanya mtihani mpaka ulipe karo yote.
sw.note: ku-fanya mtihani = to sit an exam.

en.text: There's no class today. The lecturer is away.
Yes, come in and sit down.
Come to my office tomorrow at ten.

sw.text: Njoo ofisini kwangu kesho saa nne asubuhi.
sw.note: Ten in the morning is saa nne asubuhi.

en.text: You have ninety minutes. Start now.
You can keep it for two weeks.

sw.text: Unaweza kukaa nacho kwa wiki mbili.
sw.note: na-cho = with it (the book, kitabu).

en.text: Visitors must leave by ten at night.

sw.text: Wageni wanatakiwa kuondoka kabla ya saa nne usiku.

en.text: The gate is locked at eleven at night.

sw.note: hu- = usually, every time: hu-fungwa, is locked.

en.text: Congratulations on graduating.
Sorry I'm late. There was a traffic jam.

sw.text: Samahani kwa kuchelewa. Kulikuwa na msongamano wa magari.
sw.note: Most Kenyans just say jam for traffic: kulikuwa na jam.

en.text: You're late again today.

sw.note: -me- marks a state you are in now: umechelewa (late), nimechoka (tired).

en.text: Come to my office, please.

sw.note: Njoo is 'come' to one person; to a group, njooni.

en.text: I'm coming. Should I bring anything?

sw.note: Ni-let-e: the -e ending asks 'should I bring?'.

en.text: Do you have a moment?

sw.note: Nafasi = free time or space; una nafasi? is 'are you free?'.

en.text: What time is the meeting?
Where will the meeting be?
The meeting has been moved to two in the afternoon.

sw.text: Mkutano umesogezwa hadi saa nane mchana.
sw.note: Saa nane mchana is two in the afternoon: hours count from dawn.

en.text: I'll be a bit late. Start without me.

sw.note: Anzeni: the -ni ending speaks to a group.

en.text: I'd like to add something.

sw.note: Kuchangia (to contribute) is the usual word for speaking up in meetings.

en.text: I agree with you.

sw.note: Nawe is na + wewe: with you.

en.text: I have a question about the budget.
Can we postpone the meeting to tomorrow?
The manager is in a meeting.
When will the report be ready?
I'll send it by twelve noon.

sw.text: Nitaituma kabla ya saa sita mchana.
sw.note: Nita-i-tuma: i- stands for ripoti. Saa sita mchana is twelve noon.

en.text: I've almost finished the report.
I need one more day to finish the report.

sw.text: Nahitaji siku moja zaidi kumaliza ripoti.

en.text: Good. Bring the report with you.

sw.note: Kuja na (come with) is how Kiswahili says 'bring along'.

en.text: I've sent you the email.

sw.note: Many people simply say email: nimekutumia email.

en.text: Did you get my email?
I haven't seen it. Please send it again.

sw.note: Si-ja-i-ona: -ja- means not yet; i- stands for barua pepe.

en.text: The printer isn't working.

sw.note: Haifanyi kazi (it isn't working) fits any machine: simu, gari, printa.

en.text: There's no paper in the printer.
The paper is stuck in the printer.
Please make three copies of this letter.

sw.text: Tafadhali nitolee nakala tatu za barua hii.
sw.note: Kutoa nakala = to make copies; ni-tol-ee = for me.

en.text: The system has been down since morning.

sw.note: Mfumo (system) takes u-: mfumo haufanyi kazi.

en.text: When will the system be back?

sw.note: Said like stima itarudi lini? (when will the power be back?).

en.text: They're fixing it right now.

sw.note: Wa-na-u-rekebisha: u- stands for mfumo (the system).

en.text: The internet is very slow today.

sw.note: Mtandao means both the internet and the phone network.

en.text: I'd like to take three days off next week.

sw.text: Naomba likizo ya siku tatu wiki ijayo.

en.text: Fill in the leave form first.
I filled it in yesterday.

sw.note: Nili-i-jaza: i- stands for fomu (the form).

en.text: Who will do your work while you're on leave?

sw.text: Nani atafanya kazi yako ukiwa likizo?
sw.note: U-ki-wa: -ki- means 'while' or 'if'.

en.text: My colleague will handle my work.

sw.note: Mwenzangu = my fellow, used for colleagues and classmates.

en.text: Okay, I've approved it. Enjoy your leave.

sw.note: Likizo njema is a wish, like safari njema (have a good trip).

en.text: I'm sick today. I can't come to work.

alt: Leo sijisikii vizuri. Siwezi kuja kazini.
sw.note: Naumwa = I'm unwell; naumwa kichwa = my head hurts.

en.text: So sorry. Rest and get better.

sw.note: Pole is sympathy, not an apology.

en.text: I have a doctor's appointment this afternoon.

sw.text: Nina miadi na daktari leo mchana.

en.text: Can I leave at three this afternoon?

sw.text: Leo naweza kuondoka saa tisa mchana?
alt: Naomba kuondoka leo saa tisa mchana.
sw.note: Saa tisa mchana is three in the afternoon: hours count from dawn.

en.text: Yes, but finish the report first.
Where are we eating lunch today?
Let's go eat. I'm very hungry.

sw.note: Tu-ka-le: -ka- adds 'go and': let's go and eat.

en.text: Shall I bring you something?

sw.note: Ni-ku-let-ee = I-you-bring-for.

en.text: Bring me a chapati and tea.
I brought food from home.

sw.note: Kubeba chakula (carry food) is how people say they packed lunch.

en.text: Your visitor is here.
Tell them to wait a few minutes.

sw.note: M-wambie: m- stands for one person, a man or a woman.

en.text: Tell them I'll call back later.
Please call the client.

sw.note: Kupiga simu = to phone; mpigie simu = give them a call.

en.text: The client wants to meet tomorrow.
I've finished the work you gave me.

sw.note: U-li-yo-ni-pa = you-did-which-me-give.

en.text: You did a great job.
What should I do now?

sw.note: Ni-fany-e: the -e ending asks 'should I?'.

en.text: I'm working on it right now.

sw.note: Na-i-shughulikia: i- stands for kazi (the task).

en.text: I'll finish it before I go home.
Can you show me how to use this?

sw.text: Unaweza kunionyesha jinsi ya kutumia hii?

en.text: Can I borrow your pen?
Congratulations on your promotion.

sw.note: Kupandishwa cheo = to be raised in rank: promoted.

en.text: Has the salary come in?

sw.note: Kuingia (to go in) is used for money reaching your account.

en.text: Salary is paid at the end of the month.

sw.note: Hu- means it always happens: hulipwa, is paid every time.

en.text: Can you stay until seven tonight?

sw.text: Leo unaweza kubaki hadi saa moja usiku?
sw.note: Saa moja usiku is seven in the evening: hours count from dawn.

en.text: Sorry, I have to pick up my children.

sw.note: Ni-ka-wa-chukue: -ka- adds 'go and'; wa- stands for the children.

en.text: Okay, I'll ask someone else.
Thank you for understanding.
Are you still here?
Yes, I'm finishing this first.
Please switch off the lights when you leave.

sw.note: Zima = switch off; washa = switch on.

en.text: I'm going home now.

sw.note: Nakwenda keeps ku- in careful speech; naenda is the everyday short form.

en.text: Welcome. Pick what you want.

sw.note: U-na-cho-taka: -cho- means 'the thing that': what you want.

en.text: How much is a heap of tomatoes?

sw.text: Fungu la nyanya ni bei gani?
sw.note: Fungu = a small heap sold at one price, the stall way.

en.text: Fifty. They came from the farm today.

sw.note: Zi- stands for nyanya (tomatoes).

en.text: Onions are one hundred and twenty a kilo.

sw.text: Vitunguu ni mia moja na ishirini kwa kilo.

en.text: Your tomatoes are too expensive today.

sw.text: Nyanya zako ni ghali sana leo.

en.text: Tomatoes have gone up at the market this week.

sw.text: Nyanya zimepanda bei sokoni wiki hii.
sw.note: Kupanda bei = to go up in price; kushuka bei = to come down.

en.text: The shop next door sells for less.

sw.text: Duka la jirani linauza kwa bei rahisi.
sw.note: Duka takes li-: duka la jirani linauza.

en.text: Nobody here has cheaper prices than me.

sw.text: Hakuna mwenye bei nafuu kuliko mimi hapa.
sw.note: Bei nafuu = a fair, low price.

en.text: I can't go any lower.
At that price I make no profit.
Okay, you can have it for eighty.
Take three for one hundred.
Okay, give me two heaps.

sw.note: Fungu, mafungu: ma- words take mawili for two.

en.text: What else can I get you?
Okay. Add a little extra for me.

sw.note: Niongezee is how buyers ask for a little extra, free.

en.text: Okay, I've added a little for you.
I'll give you one extra for free.

sw.note: Ni-ta-ku-ongez-ea = I-will-you-add-for.

en.text: These mangoes are sweet. Taste one.

sw.text: Maembe haya ni matamu. Onja moja.
sw.note: Embe takes ma- in the plural: maembe haya ni matamu.

en.text: Weigh it again, please.
Look, the scale shows one kilo.

sw.note: Mzani (scale) takes u-: mzani unaonyesha.

en.text: Shall I wrap it for you?

sw.note: Ni-ku-fung-ie = I-you-wrap-for.

en.text: Do you have sugar?
The sugar is finished. There'll be some tomorrow.

sw.note: Itakuwepo = it will be there, in stock.

en.text: Do you have cooking oil?
Only the small bottles are left.
Do you have a till number?
Okay, use the till number.

sw.note: A till is the shop's own M-Pesa number for payments.

en.text: Done. Did you get the message?

sw.note: Tayari = ready or done; people say it the moment a payment goes.

en.text: The money hasn't come in yet.

sw.note: Ha-i-ja-ingia: -ja- means not yet.

en.text: Wait a little, the network is slow.
Yes, the money has come in. Thank you.

sw.note: Pesa can take i- or zi-: pesa imeingia, pesa zimeingia.

en.text: Sorry, I only have big notes.
Don't you have a smaller note?
Wait, let me find change next door.

sw.note: Ni-ka-tafute: -ka- adds 'go and': let me go and find.

en.text: Here's your change.

sw.note: Hii hapa = here it is; use it for anything you hand over.

en.text: Can I pay you tomorrow?
You still owe me two hundred.

sw.note: Na-ku-dai: I claim from you, so you owe me.

en.text: Oh, I forgot. I'll send it all right now.

sw.text: Aa, nilisahau. Nitatuma yote sasa hivi.

en.text: Wait, let me check my book.

sw.note: Many small shops keep what regulars owe in a daftari.

en.text: Pay the old debt first.
Give it to me on credit. I'll pay on Friday.

sw.note: Kukopesha = to give on credit; nikopeshe = let me owe you.

en.text: Sorry, these days I don't give credit.
Can you keep it for me until evening?
Okay, I'll keep it for you.
Can you deliver to my house?
Yes, I'll send it with a boda for fifty.

sw.text: Ndiyo, nitakutumia na bodaboda kwa hamsini.
sw.note: A bodaboda is a motorbike taxi; people also say boda.

en.text: What time do you open?
I open at six in the morning.

sw.text: Nafungua saa kumi na mbili asubuhi.
sw.note: Saa kumi na mbili (hour twelve) is six in the morning: hours count from dawn.

en.text: I close at nine at night.

sw.note: Saa tatu usiku is nine at night.

en.text: On Sundays I open after the church service.

sw.note: Ibada = a church or mosque service.

en.text: Sorry, I'm closing now.
I need ten trays of eggs.
When will the stock arrive?

sw.note: Mzigo (a load) is what traders call a delivery of stock.

en.text: The lorry will arrive on Thursday morning.

sw.note: Lori takes li-, like gari: lori litafika.

en.text: One tray is missing.
Some of the eggs are broken.

sw.note: Mayai is a ma- word: mayai mengine yamevunjika.

en.text: Your price has gone up again?
I'll pay half now and half next week.

sw.text: Nitalipa nusu sasa na nusu wiki ijayo.

en.text: Where is your business permit?

sw.text: Leseni yako ya biashara iko wapi?
sw.note: Traders often just call the county business permit leseni.

en.text: Here is my permit.
Have you paid the market fee today?

sw.note: Ushuru is the daily fee the county charges traders.

en.text: I paid the fee this morning.

sw.note: Nili-lipa: -li- for a past event with a time (leo asubuhi).

en.text: Here is the receipt.
How much is the market fee per day?

sw.text: Ushuru wa soko ni pesa ngapi kwa siku?

en.text: Fifty shillings a day.
There were few customers today.
I sold everything today.
Today I made three thousand shillings.
I brought new stock today.
Are you hiring?

sw.note: Literally: are you (all) looking for workers?

en.text: I'm looking for work.
Is there any casual work today?

sw.note: kibarua = casual work, paid by the day.

en.text: I can do any kind of work.
Is the manager in?

sw.note: yupo = is here (for a person).

en.text: I saw the job advert online.
Is the job still available?
Who should I give my CV to?

sw.note: ni-m-pe = I-him/her-give: who should I give it to?

en.text: I've brought my CV.

sw.note: Kenyans just say CV (si-vi); the formal word is wasifu.

en.text: I'm here for the ten o'clock interview.

sw.text: Nimekuja kwa usaili wa saa nne.
sw.note: usaili = a job interview. Ten in the morning is saa nne.

en.text: What time is the interview?
I'm calling about last week's interview.

sw.text: Napiga simu kuhusu usaili wa wiki iliyopita.

en.text: When will you let me know?

sw.note: m-ta-ni-julisha = you (all)-will-me-inform.

en.text: Did I get the job?
I finished secondary school two years ago.

sw.text: Nilimaliza shule ya upili miaka miwili iliyopita.
sw.note: Kenyans also say kidato cha nne, Form Four, for the last year.

en.text: I have a diploma in catering.
I have three years' experience.
I was a waiter for two years.

sw.note: mhudumu = a waiter or attendant, man or woman.

en.text: The hotel closed down last year.

sw.note: mwaka jana = last year.

en.text: I don't have experience, but I learn fast.
I can drive, and I have a licence.

sw.text: Najua kuendesha gari, na nina leseni.

en.text: I'm hardworking and honest.
I'm good with customers.

sw.note: ku-wa-hudumia: -wa- is 'them', the customers.

en.text: Yes, I can work on weekends.
I'm ready to start any time.
Yes, I can carry heavy things.

sw.note: vi-tu vi-zito: the vi- sound repeats to agree.

en.text: How much is the pay?
Do you pay daily or monthly?

sw.text: Mnalipa kila siku au kila mwezi?

en.text: Can you add a little more?
Do workers get lunch?

sw.note: chakula cha mchana = lunch (food of midday).

en.text: Is overtime paid?

sw.note: saa za ziada = extra hours. Many people just say overtime.

en.text: When is payday?

sw.note: Literally: on what date does the salary come out?

en.text: What time do you start and finish?

sw.text: Mnaanza saa ngapi na mnamaliza saa ngapi?

en.text: Is there a day off each week?

sw.text: Kuna siku ya mapumziko kila wiki?

en.text: Is it a permanent job?
Is there a contract to sign?
What work will I be doing?
I can start on Monday.
When do I start?

sw.note: ni-anz-e: the -e ending asks 'should I'.

en.text: What should I wear on the first day?
What should I bring on Monday?
Thank you for the opportunity.
I'll be on time.
Do you need a copy of my ID?
I got the job. I start on Monday.
Where do I keep my things?
Who will show me the work?
Is this how you want it?

sw.note: ndivyo ... -vyo- = this is how.

en.text: Yes, we need a waiter.
Sorry, we're not hiring right now.
Please introduce yourself.

sw.note: ji- = yourself: ji-tambulishe, make yourself known.

en.text: Do you have any experience?
Why should we hire you?
Can you work on weekends?
When can you start?
The pay is twenty thousand a month.

sw.text: Mshahara ni elfu ishirini kwa mwezi.
sw.note: elfu ishirini = thousand twenty: twenty thousand.

en.text: We can only add two thousand.
Do you have a certificate of good conduct?

sw.note: Many Kenyan employers ask for this police certificate.

en.text: We'll call you next week.
Sorry, the job has already been filled.

sw.note: -mesha- = already: i-mesha-jazwa, it has already been filled.

en.text: Can you carry heavy loads?
It's six hundred a day. We pay every evening.

sw.text: Ni mia sita kwa siku. Tunalipa kila jioni.

en.text: Come on Monday at eight in the morning.

sw.note: Eight in the morning is saa mbili asubuhi.

en.text: Wear black shoes and a white shirt.

sw.text: Vaa viatu vyeusi na shati jeupe.
sw.note: vy-eusi agrees with viatu; j-eupe agrees with shati.

en.text: This is where you'll be working.

sw.note: ndipo ... -po- = this is where.

en.text: Lunch break is at one.
